description: We are a Saudi-based virtual team interested in science, engineering, and space exploration. Our goal is to use NASA resources to develop a practical solution and communicate it clearly through research, design, and a focused presentation. We welcome collaborative teammates who can contribute to coding, data analysis, or visual design.
summary: SELENE Mission Window is a working, browser-based prototype for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It combines NASA/JPL Horizons Sun-Earth ephemerides with LRO/LOLA terrain to test how landing location, date, local horizons, and lander resources affect a mission. Beyond displaying illumination and potential direct-to-Earth visibility, it simulates battery reserve and a finite science recorder across nine nearby positions. A bounded search identifies the smallest tested change to battery, solar area, recorder size, landing date, or mast height that satisfies the modeled constraints. In one reproducible Shackleton scenario, the battery remains full while a 4 GB recorder loses 2.408 GB; a 7 GB recorder prevents overflow. Users can inspect terrain, replay timelines, compare sites and dates, and export assumptions and results. This research prototype makes trade-offs visible while distinguishing NASA inputs, engineering assumptions, numerical checks, and unvalidated mission risks.
details:
Problem and intended users

Mission designers and learners need to compare what a lunar site enables over time. Average illumination alone does not establish energy sufficiency, and geometric Earth visibility alone does not ensure science can be retained and returned. A finite recorder can overflow during a communication outage even with abundant power.

What we built

SELENE Mission Window is a working software prototype with three curated south-polar study locations, selectable landing date and time, 3/7/14-day missions, an actual terrain mesh, Sun/Earth horizon views, a replayable resource timeline, nine-position sensitivity tests, an 84-combination site/date search, a bounded one-variable repair search, and downloadable mission JSON. Calculations run in the browser after loading bundled NASA-derived data; no API key or external AI service is needed at runtime.

NASA data and method

We downloaded NASA GSFC LOLA 80 m and 240 m polar elevation products and queried NASA/JPL Horizons for Sun/Earth observer ephemerides from 15 November 2026 to 1 January 2027. Spherical terrain rays extend 250 km. Each site’s 3×3 grid uses ±160 m east/north offsets and 2 m or 10 m viewpoints. We transform topocentric directions to each observer’s local frame.

Finite solar-disk exposure is approximated against the skyline at the disk center; Earth-center visibility uses an explicit clearance margin. Power integrates assumed array area, incidence, efficiency, heater, science and radio loads, battery losses and capacity. Science generation, finite recorder occupancy, overflow and conditional downlink are tracked in decimal GB.

Reproducible demonstration

At Shackleton starting 26 November 2026, 00:00 UTC for seven days, with a 3 kWh battery, 1.6 m² solar array, a 2 m viewpoint and a 4 GB recorder, all nine modeled positions maintain a full battery but none passes both energy and recorder constraints. Worst-sample overflow is 2.408 GB.

The smallest passing recorder in the +1 GB search is 7 GB: overflow becomes zero and all nine positions pass. In that worst sample, 5.688 GB reaches Earth during the interval in both cases; the larger recorder preserves 6.408 GB onboard instead of 4 GB. Retained science is not counted as returned science. A fresh 5-minute calculation finds 2.414 GB overflow and the same 7 GB decision.

Creativity and originality

Our contribution is a transparent decision workflow linking terrain-aware Sun/Earth geometry, energy and a finite science queue to explicit, testable changes. Users can investigate whether adjusting battery capacity, solar area, recorder size, landing date or mast height resolves a modeled constraint.

Lunar illumination tools, battery models and mission planning are established prior art. We do not claim the first lunar navigator or an unprecedented invention. We reviewed public tools and research; our implementation is independently written. The evidence page states overlap with prior work and the narrower differentiation.

Verification

Nine numerical test groups passed, including 324 mission runs. Checks cover energy/data conservation, an analytic darkness case, solar-disk limits, horizon wrapping, mast monotonicity, initial reserve, brownouts and timestamps. Denser radial and angular terrain sampling are checked separately.

Independent JPL observer queries at a displaced 10 m viewpoint agree within 0.000007° in azimuth and 0.000001° in elevation. These are numerical consistency checks, not spacecraft or field validation.

Limits and next work

The 80 m source grid does not resolve landing hazards. Nine points do not certify an entire landing ellipse or a success probability. Thirty-minute steps can miss short events; a 5-minute test shifts one nominal overflow onset by 45 minutes.

Earth visibility represents potential direct-to-Earth access: there is no RF budget, antenna pointing model or ground-station schedule. No descent dynamics, detailed thermal balance, dust, battery aging, radiation or structural mast qualification is modeled. Passing means only modeled battery reserve, no unmet power demand and no recorder overflow.

Future validation needs finer terrain, broader time-step convergence, radio/ground-station constraints and independent mission-tool benchmarking.

Tools, implementation status and impact

Original HTML/CSS/JavaScript with WebGL/Canvas implements the browser prototype. Python, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio and pyproj prepare NASA-derived data; Matplotlib and ReportLab create figures and PDFs.

The delivered prototype is a functioning software simulation; no physical lander was manufactured. Its intended impact is faster, inspectable early mission trade studies and education about why a bright site may still lose science.
